title: Under the Flags
passage:
The lime avenues of the older suburbs were planted a century ago, and the pavements beneath them have been losing ground ever since. A mature lime can lift a fifty-kilo flag by several centimetres in a decade – slowly enough that nobody sees it happen, steadily enough that the council’s insurers see little else. In the mid-sized city where what follows took place, compensation for trips over lifted paving costs more each year than the parks department spends on planting. The remedies have hardly changed in two generations, and every one of them points downwards. Crews grind the raised edges level. Root barriers go in around each new pit. Watering tubes are sunk a metre into the ground, on the old theory that roots chase water and can be lured away from the surface. Each measure buys a season or two. The flags keep rising.

Bronwen Askerholt, a soil scientist who has spent six years coring beneath lifted pavements, believes the remedies mistake where the problem lives. Her group lifted the flags along nineteen streets and mapped every root they found. Half a metre down, in ground compacted by machinery when the streets were first made, there was almost nothing alive: the soil was dry, airless, nearly impenetrable, and the watering tubes had made no measurable difference to it. The roots were somewhere else. In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones – where the slab cools after sunset and moisture condenses on its underside, and where air moves freely through the jointing sand – her team found dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year. “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone,” she says. “The slab shades the ground, waters it every clear night and lets it breathe. It builds the very thing that lifts it.”

The engineering answer is the root cell: an open plastic crate, stacked two or three deep beneath a rebuilt pavement and filled with loose loam. The crates, not the soil, carry the weight of the traffic above, so the loam inside is never compacted. Suppliers sell them as room to grow. Askerholt’s reading is narrower and stranger: the cells move the damp, aired horizon down and away from the stones, so that the underside of a slab stops being the best address on the street. Not everyone was persuaded. Osmund Fearnbeck, a geotechnical engineer who spent twenty years assessing tripping claims for insurers, pointed out that celled or not, the flags must still be laid on a bedding course of sand. “That course is watered and aired on exactly the terms she describes,” he wrote in a trade journal. “The roots will cross the crates and settle in the bedding. A celled pit buys time, at four times the price of an ordinary one.”

The city tried it anyway, and tried it carefully. Thirty-one streets were rebuilt on cells; the facing pavements, under the same rows of trees, were relaid in the ordinary way. For seven years both sides have been surveyed every April with a straightedge and a wedge gauge. On twenty-five streets the celled flags have stayed within tolerance while the ordinary sides opposite have been ground level twice and relaid once. One street failed and taught nobody anything: a water main was renewed halfway along it, and the trench was reinstated badly. And on five, when the flags were lifted, the crews found exactly what Fearnbeck had said they would find – mats of fine root in the bedding sand, riding clear over the crates beneath. The five had one thing in common. They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows, and the roots had evidently found it worth living in; the thin, stiff beds elsewhere were apparently not worth the climb. Those five have since been relaid on a thin mortar bed drawn up to Fearnbeck’s own specification. Askerholt’s group had thought his worry overdone. On the five streets Fearnbeck’s case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not.

The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones. Askerholt is careful about the difference. “We are reading the flags, not the roots,” she says. “For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength. The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to.” The oldest celled pavement is now in its eighth year. This April the inspectors walked it as usual, and under the lime outside number fourteen the wedge gauge showed four millimetres, the same figure as the year before. The reading went into the book.
– Sidonie Welbrace

questions.prompt: What are we told about Askerholt’s findings?

options.text: Her cores could not settle where the lifting force was coming from.
She traced most of the lift to fine roots under the stones.
Her digs showed the soil further down to be bare of living root.
Heavy anchoring roots had been cut during earlier repairs to the streets.

questions.rationale: Key B paraphrases the paragraph-2 excavation result and the load-bearing hedged quote: dense mats of fine root in the few centimetres directly beneath the stones, and “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone”. ‘She traced’ keeps the finding attributed to Askerholt, so the option does not upgrade her own hedge into narrator fact. A (over-hedge/mis-scope) tempts because the quote is hedged – but ‘could not settle where the lifting force was coming from’ contradicts the mapped result: Askerholt’s group lifted the flags along nineteen streets and mapped every root they found, so the location of the force is settled by that survey and not by the quote. C is a quantifier upgrade: the deep ground held ‘almost nothing alive’, which is not the same as soil ‘bare of living root’. D is plausible outside knowledge (root severance during repairs is a real arborist worry) that the passage never states.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the five streets in the trial?

options.text: The crates beneath them had given way under the weight of traffic.
A water main renewal, rather than the trees, seems to have disturbed them.
They had nothing obvious in common beyond their age.
They had been laid on a much deeper bed of coarse sand.

questions.rationale: Key D paraphrases the stated common feature: bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows. A fabricates a mechanical cause using passage furniture (the crates carry the traffic; nothing buckled – the roots rode over intact crates). B assigns the event in the adjacent sentence to the wrong streets: the water main wrecked ONE other street, expressly separate from the five. C contradicts ‘The five had one thing in common’: the passage identifies a shared feature rather than leaving the comparison unresolved.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the twenty-five streets in the trial?

options.text: The inspectors have measured their surfaces without examining the ground beneath.
The gauge readings taken on them have been falling year by year.
Their roots appear to have moved down into the loose loam below.
Their trees are now drawing water from beneath the road instead.

questions.rationale: Key A is the one-inch inference from paragraph 5: the streets are read every April with a straightedge and a wedge gauge, ‘The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones’, and Askerholt adds ‘We are reading the flags, not the roots’ – for all she knows the bedding on the good streets is filling with root. The evidence for the twenty-five is therefore a record of surfaces; no one has been under them since the rebuild. B fabricates a trend the surveys do not report: the eighth-year gauge reading was four millimetres, the same figure as the year before, and staying within tolerance is not a falling number. C is the inference the last paragraph exists to block – moving the damp, aired horizon down is exactly what the cells are meant to do, so a hasty reader supplies the result – but the surveys cannot see it and Askerholt refuses to sign for anything below the stones; the hedge (‘appear to have’) does not make an unobserved claim safe. D is the folk theory planted in paragraph 1 (roots chase water) precisely to be knocked down; nothing says the trees now feed under the carriageway.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude towards Fearnbeck’s objection?

options.text: She agrees with Askerholt that the worry was overdone.
She finds it mostly wrong but right on one point.
She thinks the results bore him out on the whole, with a few exceptions.
She sets out the dispute without taking a side of her own.

questions.rationale: The writer’s own verdict sentence – ‘On the five streets Fearnbeck’s case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not’ – grants Fearnbeck the bedding-course point (five streets failed exactly as he predicted, and his mortar-bed specification was adopted) while denying his general verdict that cells merely buy time. B states exactly that partial vindication. A is a role/attribution swap: ‘overdone’ was Askerholt’s group’s earlier view, which the verdict sentence pointedly does not share. C is the polarity reversal: it is two-sided in the same way as the key, so the concessive shape decides nothing, but it inverts the score – the results bore him out on five streets and refuted him on twenty-five, which is not ‘on the whole, with a few exceptions’. D is the neutral-reporter misread; a writer who scores the contest five–twenty-five has taken a side.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The rising cost to councils of people tripping over uneven paving.
Why old trees lift the paving above them, and why the remedies keep failing.
Why paving rises over tree roots, and how one city’s remedy has fared.
The case for replacing old street trees with smaller species.

questions.rationale: Whole-text gist: the passage is a mechanism story (the slab builds its own lifting layer) plus a trial of a remedy built on that mechanism, with a mixed, still-open result. C names both halves without overclaiming. A promotes the vivid paragraph-1 claims detail to main topic – and distorts it slightly (‘rising’ is not stated). B also offers a broad summary: its first half is the passage’s own mechanism, but its second half is false – the ordinary remedies of paragraph 1 do keep failing, while the celled pavements have held for seven years on twenty-five streets, so ‘the remedies keep failing’ is not what the trial reports. D is a title-plausible theme the text never argues; nobody proposes replacing the trees.

repair_log.ticket: Owner rulings 5/6: Layer-2 learner-prose scrub; exact additional edits itemised below.

edits.from: Key D paraphrases the stated common feature: bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows. The stem now names the five streets without saying what happened on them (rule 12), so nothing on the sheet gives the group away. A fabricates a mechanical cause using passage furniture (the crates carry the traffic; nothing buckled – the roots rode over intact crates). B is an actor swap from the adjacent sentence, and it is hedged (‘seems to have’) so that the cautious form is not a key signature: the water main wrecked ONE other street, expressly separate from the five. C is the cautious-sounding wrong answer – it flatly contradicts ‘The five had one thing in common’; the hedged tone is bait for the pick-the-modest-option heuristic (rule 13: here the key is the confident specific claim).
edits.to: Key D paraphrases the stated common feature: bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows. A fabricates a mechanical cause using passage furniture (the crates carry the traffic; nothing buckled – the roots rode over intact crates). B assigns the event in the adjacent sentence to the wrong streets: the water main wrecked ONE other street, expressly separate from the five. C contradicts ‘The five had one thing in common’: the passage identifies a shared feature rather than leaving the comparison unresolved.

edits.from: Whole-text gist: the passage is a mechanism story (the slab builds its own lifting layer) plus a trial of a remedy built on that mechanism, with a mixed, still-open result. C names both halves without overclaiming. A promotes the vivid paragraph-1 claims detail to main topic – and distorts it slightly (‘rising’ is not stated). B is a rival umbrella of the same breadth, so the pick-the-widest-option heuristic cannot separate it from C: its first half is the passage’s own mechanism, but its second half is false – the ordinary remedies of paragraph 1 do keep failing, while the celled pavements have held for seven years on twenty-five streets, so ‘the remedies keep failing’ is not what the trial reports. D is a title-plausible theme the text never argues; nobody proposes replacing the trees.

adversarial_blind_floors._provenance: Added in fleet-repair-4 (2026-09-01). Before this round the unit stated its floors only in gen-elf-long.NOTES.md, stated NO floor at all for q1, and stated 1-in-4 on form for q2/q3/q4 — which V-FINAL finding VF-04 refutes against verdicts-gstem-r2.jsonl, the last blind stem read executed on these bytes. Restated honestly below; every floor is at or worse than the 1-in-2 the batch16 stance-composition policy sets as its bar, so the unit stays inside policy on the measured numbers rather than on the declared ones.
adversarial_blind_floors.1: 1-in-2. Q4-A (‘She agrees with Askerholt that the worry was overdone’) presupposes, on the face of the stems sheet, that Askerholt holds a definite position on the force, which strips q1-A (‘Her cores could not settle where the lifting force was coming from’) passage-blind and leaves B vs C. The bridge is CONCEPTUAL, not lexical, so the rule-11 lemma sweep cannot see it. Only the passage separates the survivors, and it separates them on one word (‘almost’ in ‘almost nothing alive’) — the unit’s thinnest margin, VF-03 and VF-07.
adversarial_blind_floors.2: Narrowing only, no elimination. verdicts-gstem-r2.jsonl records a soft lean with ‘No firm elimination’; the stems sheet reveals that the trial has a five-street group but not what happened to it, and the blind pick (B) MISSES the key.
adversarial_blind_floors.3: 1-in-2, not the 1-in-4 previously declared. verdicts-gstem-r2.jsonl: ‘A and C are mutually undercutting … Narrowing 4->2 passage-blind.’
adversarial_blind_floors.4: Narrowing only, no elimination. Recorded by the gate as ‘this is narrowing, not answerability’: the stems sheet shows a named objector and a two-sided key shape, but not the score.
adversarial_blind_floors.5: 1-in-2. The sibling stems reveal a five-street group and a twenty-five-street group; C is then the only option covering both halves the stems disclose (verdicts-gstem-r2.jsonl).
